key_facts: Chronic, relapsing, **immune-mediated** inflammatory disease of skin, nails and joints.
Affects about **2–3%** of the UK population; onset peaks at **15–25** and **50–60** years.
Driven by the **IL-23 → Th17 → IL-17** axis: epidermis turns over in **3–5 days** instead of about 28.
Classic sign: **well-demarcated salmon-pink plaques with silvery scale** on elbows, knees, scalp and lower back.
UK care follows **NICE CG153**: emollient + potent steroid + vitamin D analogue, with planned steroid breaks; screen yearly for **psoriatic arthritis** (PEST).

sections.title: Overview
blocks: Psoriasis is a chronic, non-contagious, **immune-mediated inflammatory disease** that relapses and remits. It mainly causes sharply defined, red, scaly plaques, but it is a **multisystem** disease affecting the nails and joints and linked with cardiometabolic disease and depression.

ul: **Chronic plaque psoriasis** is the most common type (about 80–90%).
Other types: guttate, flexural (inverse), scalp, palmoplantar, nail; rare emergencies are **erythrodermic** and **generalised pustular** psoriasis.
Up to **30%** of people with psoriasis develop **psoriatic arthritis**.
Diagnosis is **clinical**; management is long term and stepped, from topicals to phototherapy, systemic drugs and biologics.

sub: About **1–3%** of the UK population (2–4% in many Western populations); up to about 4% worldwide.
Less common in tropical regions and in people of African or East Asian descent.
Can start at any age, including childhood (prevalence 0.5–2% in children).
Two onset peaks: **15–25 years** (early onset, often familial, HLA-C*06:02) and **50–60 years**.
Males and females are affected about equally.
About **one third** of patients have an affected relative.
Roughly 60% of patients have mild disease, 30% moderate and 10% severe.

sections.title: Aetiology: causes and risk factors
blocks: Psoriasis is **multifactorial**: a genetic predisposition plus environmental triggers that switch on an immune response in the skin.

ul: **HLA-C*06:02** (HLA-Cw6) is strongly linked with early-onset and guttate psoriasis (not with nail or late-onset disease).
Other susceptibility genes affect skin barrier (e.g. LCE3B/LCE3C deletion) and the IL-23/IL-17 pathway.

sub: **Streptococcal sore throat** (guttate psoriasis); **HIV** can cause severe or atypical disease.
New plaques at sites of cuts, scratches, surgery, burns, sunburn or friction.
**Beta-blockers**, **lithium**, **antimalarials** (hydroxychloroquine, chloroquine), interferons, sometimes NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors and terbinafine.
**Abrupt withdrawal of systemic (or potent topical) corticosteroids**: rebound and pustular flares.

ul: Cold, dry weather; sun usually helps, but about 10% of patients are worse with sun.

blocks.title: Drug-triggered flare after an MI
blocks.text: With post-MI polypharmacy the beta-blocker is the prime suspect, but **do not stop cardiology-critical drugs** without discussing with the GP or cardiologist.

figs.caption: Drug-triggered psoriasis: beta-blockers, lithium and antimalarials head the list.

ul: **Psoriatic arthritis** and spondyloarthropathy.
**Cardiovascular disease** and **metabolic syndrome** (obesity, hypertension, dyslipidaemia, type 2 diabetes); psoriasis is an independent cardiovascular risk factor, especially when severe.
Inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's, ulcerative colitis), uveitis, coeliac disease, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease.
**Depression and anxiety**; higher alcohol use.
NICE notes a higher **VTE** risk in severe psoriasis.

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: Psoriasis is a self-amplifying loop between immune cells and keratinocytes.

mech.k: A trigger activates the innate immune system
mech.t: Injury, infection or drugs stress keratinocytes. Plasmacytoid dendritic cells, keratinocytes and macrophages release interferon-α, TNF-α and other signals that **activate myeloid dendritic cells** in the dermis.
mech.caption: Step 1: a trigger (here a graze) activates a dendritic cell, which signals to nearby T cells.

mech.k: Dendritic cells release IL-23 and IL-12
mech.t: Activated dendritic cells produce **IL-23**, which drives the survival and expansion of **Th17** (and Th22) cells, and IL-12, which drives Th1 cells. The **IL-23/Th17 pathway** is the dominant one.
mech.caption: Step 2: dendritic-cell IL-23 expands Th17 cells, which release IL-17 and IL-22 towards the epidermis.

mech.t: Th17 cells (and γδ T cells, ILC3s, CD8 cells, neutrophils and mast cells) release **IL-17A, IL-17F and IL-22**. Keratinocytes **proliferate** and release chemokines (e.g. CCL20) and antimicrobial peptides that recruit more immune cells: a **feed-forward loop**. TNF-α amplifies every step.

mech.k: The epidermis thickens and capillaries dilate
mech.t: Keratinocytes cycle in **3–5 days instead of about 28**. The epidermis thickens (**acanthosis**) with long, regular rete ridges; papillary capillaries become dilated and tortuous, which explains the **Auspitz sign** (pinpoint bleeding when scale is removed).
mech.caption: Step 4: normal skin (left) vs psoriatic plaque (right): thick epidermis, elongated rete ridges, dilated looping capillaries and silvery scale.

mech.t: Cells reach the surface still holding their nuclei (**parakeratosis**) and fail to release the lipids that bind corneocytes, so the stratum corneum flakes off as **silvery scale**. Neutrophils collect in small pockets (**Munro microabscesses**); IL-36 overactivity tips the balance towards **pustular** psoriasis.
mech.caption: Step 5: fast-rising cells keep their nuclei (parakeratosis) and peel off as scale; neutrophils cluster in small pockets.

fig.caption: Psoriasis plaque in section: thickened epidermis, dilated capillaries and immune-cell infiltrate beneath silvery scale.

blocks.h: How treatments map onto the mechanism

ul: **Topical steroids**: broad anti-inflammatory action on the whole loop.
**Vitamin D analogues** (calcipotriol): slow keratinocyte proliferation and normalise differentiation.
**Coal tar, dithranol, salicylic acid**: antiproliferative and keratolytic.
**Phototherapy (NB-UVB)**: induces T-cell apoptosis in the skin.
**Biologics**: TNF-α inhibitors, **IL-17** inhibitors, **IL-23** (p19) and IL-12/23 (p40) inhibitors block the central cytokines; TYK2 and PDE4 inhibitors act on intracellular signalling.

histo: **Regular acanthosis** with elongated, club-shaped rete ridges.
**Parakeratosis** (retained nuclei in the stratum corneum) with loss of the granular layer.
**Munro microabscesses** (neutrophils in the stratum corneum) and **spongiform pustules of Kogoj**.
Thinned suprapapillary plates and **dilated, tortuous papillary capillaries** (Auspitz sign).
Perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate. Biopsy is only needed if the diagnosis is uncertain.

ul: **Itch** is usually mild to moderate but can be severe; scratching causes lichenification.
Painful **fissures**, especially on palms, soles and in flexures.
Scaling and shedding; **joint pain, stiffness or swelling** suggests psoriatic arthritis.
Major **psychosocial burden**: embarrassment, low mood, impact on work and relationships.

lesions.name: Well-demarcated plaque
lesions.t: Sharply defined, raised, **salmon-pink** plaque, usually symmetrical. The sharp edge helps separate it from eczema.

lesions.name: Silvery scale
lesions.t: Thick, white, micaceous scale; removing it causes pinpoint bleeding (**Auspitz sign**).

lesions.name: Koebner phenomenon
lesions.t: New lesions appear in lines along scratches or scars (also seen in lichen planus and vitiligo).

lesions.name: Post-inflammatory change
lesions.t: Plaques may leave pale or dark marks that fade over months, especially in skin of colour.

bodymap.caption: Typical sites: scalp and hairline, elbows, knees, lower back, natal cleft, umbilicus and nails; flexures in inverse psoriasis.
pts: **Scalp**, often extending just beyond the hairline and behind the ears.
**Nails** (in up to half of patients, more with arthritis).
Flexures, genitals, palms and soles in specific types.

figs.caption: Symmetrical scaly plaques on the knees.
Multiple plaques on the trunk: estimate body surface area.

variants.name: Chronic plaque
variants.t: Persistent plaques > 3 cm on extensors, scalp and lower back; from mild to very extensive.

variants.name: Guttate
variants.t: Many small **raindrop** plaques on trunk and limbs, often **2–3 weeks after a strep throat**; may clear in months or evolve into plaque disease.

variants.name: Scalp
variants.t: Thick adherent scale; often the first or only site; extends beyond the hairline.

variants.name: Flexural (inverse)
variants.t: Smooth, shiny, well-defined red patches with **little or no scale** in axillae, groin, natal cleft and under the breasts; fissure in the crease; may be colonised by Candida.

variants.name: Palmoplantar
variants.t: Well-defined scaly plaques or diffuse hyperkeratosis with painful **fissures**; disproportionately disabling.

variants.name: Nail psoriasis
variants.t: Pitting, onycholysis and oil-drop sign; a marker of higher **psoriatic arthritis** risk.

variants.name: Sebopsoriasis
variants.t: Overlap with seborrhoeic dermatitis on the scalp, face, ears and chest.

variants.name: Unstable / pustular
variants.t: Rapid extension, new plaques or pustules, often after steroid withdrawal or infection.

variants.name: Erythrodermic
variants.t: Confluent redness and scaling over **> 90%** of the skin; temperature dysregulation, fluid loss, heart failure. **Same-day** assessment.

variants.name: Generalised pustular (von Zumbusch)
variants.t: Sheets of sterile pustules on red skin with fever and malaise. **Same-day** assessment.

sub: Plaques are often thicker with more prominent grey or silvery scale and look **violaceous, grey or dark brown** rather than pink; erythema is harder to judge.
Post-inflammatory hyper- or hypopigmentation is marked and can last longer than the plaques.
Involvement is often more extensive; palmoplantar, pustular and erythrodermic forms may be more frequent.
Guttate and scalp/flexural/napkin disease are common; NICE recommends **specialist referral at presentation**.
Psoriasis often improves but may flare after delivery; acitretin and methotrexate are teratogenic (specialist planning).
Can be extensive and recalcitrant; consider HIV testing in sudden severe psoriasis.

figs.caption: Skin of colour: violaceous plaques with grey scale.
Flexural psoriasis: shiny, sharply defined, no satellites.
Psoriatic nail pitting from matrix involvement.

sections.title: Diagnosis and investigations
blocks: Diagnosis is **clinical**, based on morphology, distribution, nails and joints.

ul: Onset, course, previous treatments and response; **triggers** (sore throat, drugs, stress, steroid withdrawal).
**Joint symptoms**: pain, swelling, morning stiffness, heel pain, dactylitis.
Family history; smoking, alcohol, weight; mood; impact on work and relationships.
Morphology and **body surface area (BSA)**: the patient's palm with fingers is about 1% BSA.
**High-impact sites**: face, scalp, hands, feet, nails, genitals.
Nails, scalp, natal cleft and umbilicus for supporting clues; joints for swelling or dactylitis.

head: Tool
What it measures
rows: Extent: the patient's palm ≈ 1%. > 10% suggests moderate to severe disease.
Psoriasis Area and Severity Index (0–72): redness, thickness, scale × area; used for systemic and biologic decisions.
Static physician's or patient's global assessment (clear to severe); NICE suggests patient and clinician assessment.
Dermatology Life Quality Index (0–30); CDLQI for children.
Psoriasis Epidemiology Screening Tool: annual screen for psoriatic arthritis; score ≥ 3 → rheumatology.

ul: **Usually none.**
**Skin biopsy** if the diagnosis is uncertain (e.g. to exclude mycosis fungoides or lupus).
**Throat swab** (or ASO titre) if guttate psoriasis follows a sore throat.
**Skin scrapings and nail clippings** for mycology when tinea or onychomycosis is possible.
**Cardiovascular risk** assessment (NICE: at presentation, and at least every 5 years if severe): BP, BMI, lipids, HbA1c.
Baseline bloods before systemic therapy are arranged by the specialist team.

ddx.name: Atopic eczema
ddx.f: Ill-defined, very itchy, **flexural** in adults; lichenification; atopic history.

ddx.name: Seborrhoeic dermatitis
ddx.f: Greasy yellow scale on the central face, eyebrows, scalp and chest; less sharply defined; can overlap (sebopsoriasis).

ddx.name: Tinea corporis
ddx.f: Asymmetrical, with an **advancing scaly edge** and central clearing; scrapings positive.

ddx.name: Discoid eczema
ddx.f: Coin-shaped, very itchy, oozing or crusted plaques, often on the legs.

ddx.name: Lichen planus
ddx.f: Violaceous, flat-topped polygonal papules with **Wickham striae**; wrists, mouth.

ddx.name: Pityriasis rosea
ddx.f: Herald patch then oval patches with a **collarette** in a Christmas-tree pattern; clears in 6–12 weeks.

ddx.name: Candidal intertrigo
ddx.f: Macerated, beefy red folds with **satellite papules and pustules** (flexural psoriasis has none).

ddx.name: Hyperkeratotic hand eczema
ddx.f: Hardest to separate from palmoplantar psoriasis; patch testing or biopsy may be needed; they can coexist.

ddx.name: Palmoplantar pustulosis
ddx.f: Sterile yellow and brown pustules on palms and soles; strongly linked to smoking.

ddx.name: Mycosis fungoides
ddx.f: Persistent, atypical, often itchy patches in sun-protected sites that do not respond: biopsy.

ddx.name: Onychomycosis (nails)
ddx.f: Asymmetric, yellow, crumbly nails, often toenails; mycology positive. Psoriasis has pits.

ul: Follow **NICE CG153** and the CKS summary. Psoriasis is **chronic**: treatment is intermittent and most patients relapse after stopping.
Agree goals; consider severity, sites, impact, patient preference and comorbidities.
Explain **how much** to apply and **when** (fingertip units), planned **steroid breaks**, and how long until response (about 4 weeks for topicals).
Review **4 weeks** after starting a new topical (2 weeks in children).
Screen yearly for **psoriatic arthritis** and assess cardiovascular risk, mood and lifestyle.
**Mild**: limited plaques managed with topicals.
**Moderate to severe** (e.g. BSA > 10%, PASI ≥ 10, DLQI > 10, high-impact sites, failure of topicals): consider referral for phototherapy or systemic therapy.
**Emollients** regularly and generously: reduce scale and itch and help active topicals work.
Stop smoking; moderate alcohol; support weight loss (it can reduce severity).
Avoid skin trauma and picking; manage stress.
Seek prompt review for unexplained joint pain or swelling.
Prescribing detail for emollients: [emollients](condition:emollients).

fig.caption: One fingertip unit (about 0.5 g) treats an area the size of two adult palms.
fig.alt: Fingertip unit of cream on an index finger

drugs.name: Potent topical corticosteroid + vitamin D analogue
drugs.dose: Potent steroid **once daily** plus vitamin D analogue **once daily**, applied at different times of day, for **up to 4 weeks**.
drugs.use: First-line for chronic plaque psoriasis on trunk and limbs.
drugs.cautions: Potent steroid no longer than **8 weeks** at any one site; leave a **4-week break** between courses.
drugs.counsel: Apply to plaques only; separate the two products in time (e.g. morning and evening).

drugs.name: Vitamin D analogue (e.g. calcipotriol)
drugs.dose: **Twice daily** for 8–12 weeks if not controlled after 4 weeks of the combination above.
drugs.cautions: Irritation, especially on the face and flexures; avoid excessive amounts (hypercalcaemia).
drugs.counsel: Wash hands after use; can be used between steroid courses.

drugs.name: Calcipotriol / betamethasone dipropionate
drugs.use: Third step (or alternative to a potent steroid twice daily or coal tar) when the vitamin D analogue fails; helps adherence.
drugs.cautions: Contains a potent steroid: same duration limits and breaks. Brands vary by formulary.
drugs.counsel: Foam and gel suit the scalp and hairy areas; shake foam well.

drugs.name: Very potent topical corticosteroid
drugs.cautions: Usually on specialist advice; no longer than **4 weeks** at a site; avoid face and flexures.

drugs.name: Coal tar
drugs.use: Alternative step on trunk, limbs and scalp (shampoo).
drugs.cautions: Messy, odour, staining; coal tar shampoo alone is not enough for severe scalp disease.
drugs.counsel: Use in the evening; may stain clothes and bedding.

drugs.name: Dithranol (short-contact)
drugs.use: Hospital or specialist settings for large plaques.
drugs.cautions: Burns and stains skin and fabrics; avoid face and flexures.

ul: Start with a **potent steroid** in a suitable vehicle (lotion, gel or shampoo) for up to 4 weeks.
Next: **calcipotriol/betamethasone** combination or a vitamin D analogue.
Use a **scale softener** (e.g. salicylic acid or oil-based preparations) first for thick scale.
**Mild or moderate** potency steroid once or twice daily for **a maximum of 2 weeks**; flexures are at high risk of atrophy (about 1–2 weeks a month).
**Do not** use potent or very potent steroids here.

If response is poor or continuous steroid is needed: **topical calcineurin inhibitor** (tacrolimus or pimecrolimus) twice daily for up to 4 weeks, started by a clinician with psoriasis expertise (off-label).
Vitamin D analogues may help but can irritate; tar, dithranol and salicylic acid are usually too irritant in folds.

figs.caption: Flexural psoriasis: mild or moderate steroid short course only.
Steroid absorption varies by site: thin skin (face, eyelids, flexures, genitals) absorbs far more.

ul: Emollients and keratolytics (e.g. **salicylic acid**, urea); **potent or very potent** steroid ± vitamin D analogue or combination, with occlusion overnight.
Nail disease responds poorly to topicals; refer if severe or with joint symptoms.

drugs.name: Phototherapy (narrowband UVB; PUVA)
drugs.use: Plaque or guttate psoriasis not controlled with topicals; hand–foot PUVA for palmoplantar disease.
drugs.cautions: Cumulative skin cancer risk, especially PUVA.

drugs.name: Methotrexate
drugs.use: Moderate to severe psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis.
drugs.cautions: **Once weekly** dosing; folic acid; teratogenic; interactions (e.g. trimethoprim, NSAIDs).
drugs.monitor: FBC, LFTs, renal function; liver fibrosis assessment (specialist).

drugs.name: Ciclosporin
drugs.use: Rapid control, or when planning conception.

drugs.name: Acitretin
drugs.cautions: **Teratogenic for 3 years after stopping**: pregnancy prevention required; lipids and LFTs.

drugs.name: Biologics
drugs.cls: TNF-α, IL-17, IL-23 and IL-12/23 inhibitors
drugs.use: Severe psoriasis that has failed or cannot use conventional systemic therapy and phototherapy (NICE TAs).
drugs.cautions: Infection risk; screen for TB and hepatitis; **no live vaccines**.

blocks.title: Avoid oral steroids
blocks.text: Systemic corticosteroids are best avoided in psoriasis: withdrawal can trigger rebound, erythrodermic or pustular flares.

ladder.t: Emollients, lifestyle support, explanation and arthritis screening.
**Potent steroid OD + vitamin D analogue OD** (different times of day) to trunk and limbs; potent steroid for scalp; mild/moderate steroid for face and flexures.
**Vitamin D analogue BD** if not controlled.
**Potent steroid BD** (up to 4 weeks) or **coal tar**, or **calcipotriol/betamethasone OD** (up to 4 weeks). Plan 4-week steroid breaks.
Phototherapy, methotrexate, ciclosporin, acitretin, then small molecules and biologics.

ul: Psoriasis is linked with **depression, anxiety and suicidal ideation**; quality-of-life impact can equal other major chronic diseases.
Ask about mood, alcohol and work at reviews; use the DLQI.
Signpost support (e.g. the Psoriasis Association) and refer for psychological support when needed.

refer.t: Suspected **psoriatic arthritis**: rheumatology (urgent if active synovitis).
Diagnostic uncertainty; extensive disease or failure of topicals; major impact on quality of life; severe nail disease; all **children**.
Eligible for phototherapy or systemic therapy.

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

refer.t: Widespread redness over **90%** of the skin (erythroderma), especially with shivering, feeling unwell or fluid loss.
Sheets of **pustules** with fever (generalised pustular psoriasis), often after steroid withdrawal.
Hot, swollen joints or dactylitis (active psoriatic arthritis).
Atypical plaques not responding to treatment (exclude mycosis fungoides or lupus).

ul: **Psoriatic arthritis** (10–30%): joint damage if untreated.
**Cardiometabolic disease**: ischaemic heart disease, stroke, hypertension, diabetes, chronic kidney disease (severe disease).
**Erythroderma**: fluid and electrolyte loss, hypothermia, infection, high-output heart failure.
**Treatment-related**: steroid atrophy, striae and rebound; phototherapy skin cancer risk; systemic drug toxicity; infection on biologics.
Secondary infection in flexures (Candida, bacteria); lichenification from scratching.
Psychological: depression, alcohol misuse, social isolation.

fig.caption: Steroid atrophy: thinning of epidermis and dermis with visible vessels after prolonged potent steroid use.

ul: A **lifelong** relapsing and remitting condition; about 17–55% of patients have remissions of varying length.
Guttate psoriasis often clears within months but may later evolve into plaque disease.
Severe psoriasis is associated with reduced life expectancy (about 3–4 years), largely through cardiovascular disease.

pearls: Explain that psoriasis is **chronic** and treatment is intermittent; most patients relapse after stopping.
Demonstrate application; cosmetic acceptability drives adherence, so **gels and foams** often beat ointments for daytime use.
Spell out **steroid breaks** (4 weeks between potent courses) to prevent atrophy and rebound.
Calcipotriol/betamethasone products vary by formulary: check local brands.
**Avoid oral steroids**: withdrawal can trigger rebound or pustular flares.
Check the drug history for **beta-blockers, lithium and antimalarials**, but do not stop cardiology-critical drugs alone.
Counsel on vaccination and infection risk if the patient later moves to immunosuppression.
NICE notes a higher **VTE** risk in severe psoriasis.

quiz.q: Which cytokine axis is central to psoriasis?
How fast do keratinocytes turn over in a plaque?

quiz.a: Pinpoint bleeding when scale is removed, from dilated papillary capillaries.

quiz.q: First-line NICE topical regimen for trunk and limbs?
quiz.a: Potent steroid once daily plus vitamin D analogue once daily, at different times, for up to 4 weeks.

quiz.q: Maximum potent steroid duration at one site?
quiz.a: 8 weeks (very potent 4 weeks), with a 4-week break between courses.

quiz.q: Which steroid potency for face and flexures?
quiz.a: Mild or moderate only, for up to 2 weeks.
